summary: Extends the PIDF-LO location format (RFC 4119) so location can be described relative to a reference point, which may itself be geodetic or civic, using one of several shapes for the offset. It also describes a binary form and an optional link to a map image.

eli5.summary: Instead of an address, you say go three steps north of the big tree. It is a way to write that down.

questions: how to express location relative to a point
what is relative location in pidf-lo
how to express location as an offset from a reference point
what is the pidf-lo relative-location element
subtitle: How to say where something is as an offset in meters from a known reference point, in PIDF-LO XML or a compact binary form.

tldr.problem: Location objects can describe a place as a civic address or a geodetic shape, but not as an offset from a known point such as a front door or a building corner.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7035 adds a relative-location element to PIDF-LO holding a reference location and an offset shape measured in meters east and north of it. It also defines a binary TLV form and optional map metadata.
tldr.outcome: Clients that do not understand relative location still see the baseline location, so the baseline should be broad enough to enclose both the reference and the offset.

today: RFC 7035 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Relative Location in PIDF-LO
sections.content:
RFC 7035 extends the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO, RFC 4119) so that a location can be expressed as a reference location plus a relative offset. The reference can be civic or geodetic and can carry dynamic parts such as velocity. The offset is given in meters on a Cartesian grid.

Two formats are defined. An XML form is meant for PIDF-LO. A type-length-value (TLV) form is meant for other protocols that already carry binary location data, such as the civic address format of RFC 4776.

An optional URI can also point to a map or floor plan, with extra fields that let an application orient and scale that map correctly.
sections.eli5: It is a way to write down where something is by pointing to a known spot and saying how far away to go from it. You can also attach a map so people can see it.

sections.title: Baseline, Reference and Offset
sections.content:
A relative location has three parts. The baseline location sits outside the <relative-location> element, so a client that does not understand the extension still sees it. The reference location refines the baseline and is the starting point. The offset says where the target is, measured from the reference.

Creators choose how much detail goes in each. For example, the baseline can be precise enough to name a building, and the reference can be a point inside that building. Location objects SHOULD NOT put all their information in the baseline, because older clients would treat the reference point as the target's actual precise location. The baseline SHOULD be as accurate as possible while still enclosing both the reference and the relative location.

If the baseline is geodetic, the reference MUST be geodetic. If the baseline is a civic address, the reference MUST be civic. Baseline and reference MAY also carry dynamic location information from RFC 5962.

A valid relative location can have nothing in the baseline, but then recipients that do not understand relative location learn nothing at all.
sections.eli5: The baseline is a big circle on the map that includes everything. The reference is a spot inside it, and the offset says how far from that spot you really are.

sections.title: The Relative Coordinate System
sections.content:
The reference location is the origin of the coordinate system. If the reference has uncertainty, its centroid is used. The first axis (x) increases toward the East, the second (y) points North, and the optional third (z) points Up. Every axis is in meters. Angles are in degrees, measured from North toward East, with zero at North.

In XML the two-dimensional system is named urn:ietf:params:geopriv:relative:2d and the three-dimensional one urn:ietf:params:geopriv:relative:3d. In binary, 2D and 3D shapes use different type codes.

Dynamic information in the baseline or reference rotates the axes so the y axis follows the <orientation> element, and the system moves as described by <speed> and <heading>. A single timestamp covers the baseline, the reference and the relative location together, and the location generator is responsible for keeping them consistent.

Only one relative shape MUST be included for a given reference point. Any error in the reference point carries over into the final location.
sections.eli5: It is like graph paper laid on the ground with the reference spot at the middle. Right is east, up the page is north, and each square is one meter.

sections.title: Offset Shapes
sections.content:
The offset is a shape in the relative coordinate system, written in GML as in RFC 5491. The RFC defines nine shape type codes in binary: point, circle, sphere, ellipse, ellipsoid, polygon (2D and 3D) and prism, plus the arc-band.

  • Point: one set of coordinates with unknown uncertainty (2 values in 2D, 3 in 3D).
  • Circle or sphere: a point plus one radius in meters.
  • Ellipse or ellipsoid: a point plus semi-major and semi-minor axes and an orientation, with a semi-vertical axis added in 3D.
  • Polygon or prism: a boundary of at least 3 points; a prism adds an altitude per point and a height. Encodings SHOULD use 15 or fewer points unless the recipient is known to support more.
  • Arc-band: a region bounded by inner and outer radii and a start and opening angle. It exists only in a 2D system.

A GML polygon repeats its first point at the end, but the TLV form removes the duplicate, and the point count is inferred from the TLV length. A polygon with altitude cannot be represented perfectly in TLV form: the conversion drops to 2D and removes altitude.
sections.eli5: You can say you are exactly at a spot, or somewhere inside a circle, an oval, a many-sided shape or a slice of a ring around it. The shape shows how sure you are.

sections.title: The Binary TLV Form
sections.content:
The binary form uses a type-length-value tuple. The Type is an 8-bit unsigned integer and the Length is an 8-bit unsigned integer counting only the Value bytes. Type codes come from a new IANA registry that is not allowed to collide with the civic address types (CAtypes), so a reference and an offset can sit in one object.

The reference TLV uses code 111 and wraps the baseline and reference as civic TLVs or geo TLVs, depending on the baseline. The offset and optional map TLVs follow it. Shapes use codes 113 to 122, and dynamic elements use 123 (orientation), 124 (speed) and 125 (heading).

Coordinates, distances and angles are single-precision IEEE 754 floating-point values: 32 bits with a sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fractional bits. A value that cannot be represented exactly MUST be encoded as the best approximation, following Clinger 1990.
sections.eli5: The binary form packs everything into little labeled boxes: a label, a length, then the contents. Each kind of shape has its own label number.

sections.title: Map Metadata
sections.content:
An optional <map> element gives a recipient a visual reference. The RFC does not say how the recipient uses it. The URL MUST be http: or https: unless the creator can ensure that authorized recipients can use other schemes, and a type attribute holding a MIME media type MUST be present. In binary, the media type is TLV 126 and the URL is TLV 127.

Three optional fields tie the map to the relative grid. The offset (TLV 129) gives the reference point's coordinates in the map. For images, coordinates start at the upper left, counted by column and then by row. The orientation (TLV 130) is degrees relative to North, and defaults to zero. The scale (TLV 131) is one factor per axis, such as pixels per meter, and a negative y value can account for image rows that run downward.

Because the binary form limits data to 255 octets, applications using XML that cannot rule out a binary form are encouraged to keep the URL within that size.
sections.eli5: You can staple a picture of the floor plan to the note, and say where the starting spot is on the picture, which way is north, and how big a meter is on it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Privacy for location data is typically important. Relative location may increase precision but does not otherwise change the privacy considerations discussed in RFC 4119.

The main new risk is the map URL. Fetching it can reveal information, since the map's coverage area or the URL parameters could hint at the target's location, and the target and the location recipient are often the same entity. Access to map URLs MUST be secured with TLS (an https URI) unless the URL cannot leak information about the target. If the URL tells a map server more than it is authorized to know, the URL MUST NOT be included in the PIDF-LO.

IANA is asked to create the "Relative Location Parameters" registry (IETF Review), register an XML namespace and schema, and create a "Geopriv Identifiers" registry holding the two relative CRS URNs.
sections.eli5: Looking at a map picture can tell the map's owner roughly where you are. So the map link should use a secure connection, or be left out if it would give away too much.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF A RELATIVE LOCATION

items.title: Baseline
items.text: Outside the relative element, so clients that ignore the extension still see it. Should enclose both reference and target.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Refines the baseline and is the origin of the offset. Civic if the baseline is civic, geodetic if it is geodetic.

items.title: Offset
items.text: A shape in meters east and north (and up in 3D) of the reference.

items.label: Orientation
items.desc: Dynamic location; one or two angles.

items.label: Heading
items.desc: Dynamic location; one or two angles.

items.label: Map type
items.desc: MIME media type of the map.

items.label: Map coordinates
items.desc: Reference point as it appears in the map.

items.label: Map angle
items.desc: Map orientation in degrees from North.

items.label: Map scale
items.desc: One scale value per axis, or a single value.
